about: Verified against the exact-version PDFs required by The Relay brief on 2026-11-10: Attention Is All You Need v7, Moshi v1, and Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling v2. Q6, Q11, Q12, Q15 and Q19 wording/key notes were tightened during verification. All 20 questions have verified=true. Post-verification fixes (author, 2026-11-10): Q12 'Large H-Net matches XL BPE' moved from required to optional; Q15 decoder point also accepts HNET §2.1.2 and §2.3, where the sentence it paraphrases appears.

grading_rule.decided_by: author, 2026-11-10 (strict); citation rule amended by author, 2026-11-10
grading_rule.correct: Answerable question: EVERY required point is present and right, and each claim carries a citation to a passage that supports it.
grading_rule.point_rule: Amended by the author 2026-11-11 ('drop down the strictness a bit'): a required point counts when its main idea is stated correctly; specific details inside it (numbers, names, formulas, secondary clauses) are required only when the question asks for them. Wrong facts and unsupported citations still make an answer wrong.
grading_rule.citation_rule: A citation counts if the cited passage actually supports the claim. The 'cites' listed for each point are a guide to where the support is, not an exhaustive allowed set: papers repeat facts across the abstract, introduction and method sections. A cite to a passage that does not support the claim is still wrong.
grading_rule.diagnostic_not_a_grade: For each answerable question, the grader also records required-point coverage (points covered / points required) in trace.jsonl. It is not written to results.csv and does not change answer_grade; it is only used to explain differences between retrieval settings in the write-up, labelled as coming from the trace.
grading_rule.wrong: Answerable question: any required point missing, any stated fact wrong (including a forbidden value from 'traps'), or a claim cited to a passage that does not support it. Unanswerable question: anything other than a refusal, i.e. the asked quantity is given or guessed.
grading_rule.refused_correctly: Unanswerable question: the answer says the three papers do not establish the asked information and gives no value for it. Adjacent facts may be mentioned only if cited and explicitly framed as not answering the question.
grading_rule.refused_wrongly: Answerable question: the system refuses or says the papers do not cover it.

cite_format: PAPER §section | PAPER Table N | PAPER Figure N | PAPER Abstract, with PAPER in {AIAYN, MOSHI, HNET}

required.point: For large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude
required.level_why: asks 'why are the ... dot products divided' - growth with d_k is the why

required.point: This pushes the softmax into regions with extremely small gradients
required.level_why: asks 'What problem does this scaling prevent?'

required.point: Dot products are scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k) to counteract this
required.level_why: the scaling itself is the subject of the question

optional: Footnote: if q and k components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, q·k has mean 0 and variance d_k
Without scaling, additive attention outperforms dot-product attention for larger d_k
traps: The paper says the authors 'suspect' this; stating it as proven is acceptable but should not add reasons the paper does not give

required.point: Encoder self-attention: queries, keys and values all come from the output of the previous encoder layer; each position attends to all positions
required.level_why: asks to 'explain ... encoder self-attention'

required.point: Decoder self-attention: each position attends only to positions up to and including itself, enforced by masking (setting to -inf) illegal connections in the softmax input
required.level_why: asks to explain 'masked decoder self-attention'

required.point: Encoder-decoder attention: queries from the previous decoder layer, keys and values from the encoder output; every decoder position attends over all input positions
required.level_why: asks to explain 'encoder-decoder attention'

required.point: Masking prevents leftward information flow to preserve the auto-regressive property: with output embeddings offset by one, predictions for position i depend only on known outputs at positions < i
required.level_why: asks 'Why is masking necessary in the decoder?'

optional: Figure 2 shows the mask inside scaled dot-product attention

required.point: Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks; same dimension d_model so they can be summed
required.level_why: asks 'How does it incorporate positional information'

required.point: They use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies (PE(pos,2i)=sin(pos/10000^(2i/d_model)), PE(pos,2i+1)=cos(...)); wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π
required.level_why: the sinusoidal functions are how; the question names them
required.level2_parts: the PE formula; wavelengths in a geometric progression from 2pi to 10000*2pi

required.point: Learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results (Table 3 row (E))
required.level_why: 'despite observing nearly identical results' is given in the question as a premise, not asked

required.point: Sinusoidal was chosen because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen in training
required.level_why: asks 'Why did the authors choose sinusoidal'

optional: Hypothesis: lets the model attend by relative position, since PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos)
Table 3 row (E): PPL 4.92, BLEU 25.7 vs base 4.92 / 25.8
traps: The extrapolation reason is a 'may allow', not a demonstrated result

required.point: N = 6 layers (encoder and decoder each)
required.level_why: listed: 'Number of encoder and decoder layers'

required.point: d_model = 512
required.level_why: listed: 'Model dimension (d_model)'
listed: 'Feed-forward dimension (d_ff)'

required.point: h = 8 heads
required.level_why: listed: 'Number of attention heads'

required.point: d_k = 64 and d_v = 64
required.level_why: listed: 'Key and value dimensions'

required.level_why: listed: 'Number of training steps'

'Table 3' exists in all three papers (MOSHI Table 3 is a Mimi ablation, HNET Table 3 is HellaSwag robustness)

required.point: Limitation 1, latency: it compounds along the pipeline's components, giving a global latency of several seconds (vs a few hundred ms in natural conversation)
required.level_why: asks 'What are these three limitations' (latency)
required.level2_parts: 'a few hundred ms in natural conversation'

required.point: Limitation 2, text bottleneck: understanding and generation happen in text, so non-written information (paralinguistics such as emotion and accent, non-speech audio) is lost
required.level_why: the three limitations (text bottleneck)
required.level2_parts: the examples emotion, accent, non-speech audio

required.point: Limitation 3, turn-based modeling: assumes well-defined single-speaker segments, so it cannot model interruptions, overlapping speech and backchanneling
required.level_why: the three limitations (turn-based)

required.point: Moshi casts dialogue as speech-to-speech generation in the audio domain on top of a text LLM backbone (Helium), removing the text bottleneck
required.level_why: asks 'how does Moshi's speech-to-speech approach attempt to address them' (text bottleneck)

required.point: Streaming hierarchical architecture with theoretical latency 160 ms (200 ms in practice)
required.level_why: how Moshi addresses latency: streaming, low latency

required.point: Multi-stream modeling of its own and the user's audio removes the speaker-turn concept, allowing overlap and interruptions
required.level_why: how Moshi addresses turn-taking: multi-stream, no speaker turns

optional: Overlapping speech is 10 to 20% of spoken time
Natural conversation average response time 230 ms across 10 languages

required.point: The two audio streams are Moshi's own speech and the user's speech; they are represented as distinct parallel streams but jointly modelled in one multi-sequence, not generated as two independent dialogue systems.
required.level_why: asks 'What are the two audio streams - whose speech is represented in each'

required.point: The acoustic delay is applied to both streams and they are concatenated into the jointly modeled multi-sequence
required.level_why: asks 'how are these distinct streams jointly modelled': both concatenated into one jointly modelled sequence
required.level2_parts: the acoustic delay applied to both

required.point: There are no explicit turn boundaries: the model always listens and always generates (speech or silence), i.e. full-duplex
required.level_why: asks how they 'support simultaneous listening and speaking'

required.point: At inference Moshi's stream is sampled while the user's predicted stream is replaced by the real user audio
required.level_why: inference-time replacement of the user stream by real audio is not asked

required.point: Because there is no speaker-turn segmentation, overlap and interruptions can be modeled
required.level_why: asks how they support 'overlapping speech and interruptions'

optional: Predicting the user stream too enables simulated dialogues for offline evaluation
Total K = 2Q+1 = 17 streams including the text stream
traps: Do not say the streams are modelled independently: the paper applies delays to both streams and concatenates them into the jointly modelled sequence.
The text (Inner Monologue) stream is only for Moshi's speech, not the user's.

required.point: Mimi is an autoencoder (SeaNet with Transformers) with a residual vector quantization bottleneck: 24 kHz audio to 12.5 Hz latents, Q = 8 quantizers with codebook size 2048
required.level_why: asks 'What role do residual vector quantization ... play': an autoencoder with an RVQ bottleneck
required.level2_parts: SeaNet; 24 kHz -> 12.5 Hz; Q = 8; codebook size 2048

required.point: Semantic information is distilled from WavLM into the first quantizer level using a cosine distance
required.level_why: asks the role of 'knowledge distillation': WavLM distilled into the first quantizer level

required.point: Split RVQ: distillation into a single RVQ's first level hurt audio quality, so semantic information goes into a plain VQ and acoustic information into a 7-level RVQ in parallel, with outputs summed
required.level_why: asks 'how Mimi combines semantic and acoustic information': split RVQ, semantic VQ + acoustic RVQ
required.level2_parts: 7 levels; outputs summed; why a single RVQ hurt quality

required.point: All convolutions are causal, so Mimi encodes and decodes in streaming fashion: an 80 ms frame yields a latent step that decodes to 80 ms of audio, which makes real-time generation possible
required.level_why: asks 'why is Mimi's causal design important for real-time speech generation'

optional: Bitrate 1.1 kbps
Quantization applied only 50% of the time during training
Non-causal pooling of WavLM targets is fine because it is only used in training
traps: The latent is 512-d but projected to 256-d before RVQ

required.point: Inner Monologue: Moshi also models the text of its own speech as a time-aligned text stream inserted as a prefix to the semantic tokens
required.level_why: asks 'What is the Inner Monologue technique' and how text tokens are incorporated (time-aligned prefix to semantic tokens)

required.point: Alignment: Whisper word-level timestamps are mapped to the 12.5 Hz frames, with PAD and EPAD special tokens filling the gaps between words
required.level_why: asks 'how time-aligned text tokens are incorporated into audio generation' (author's edit)
required.level1_main: Text tokens are temporally aligned with the audio frames and incorporated into the generated multi-stream sequence.
required.level2_parts: Whisper word-level timestamps; the PAD and EPAD names; the exact 12.5 Hz alignment; the specific padding mechanism between words

required.point: It provides scaffolding that increases the linguistic quality of generated speech
required.level_why: asks 'why this improves linguistic quality'

required.point: Delay controls which modality decides content: audio ahead of text (sample only text with real audio) gives streaming ASR; text ahead of audio gives streaming TTS
required.level_why: asks how 'changing the delay ... allows ... streaming ASR and TTS'

optional: Padding tokens are about 65% of text tokens in English conversational speech
The user's speech is not transcribed

required.level_why: listed

required.level_why: listed

required.level_why: listed

required.level_why: listed

required.level_why: listed

'Table 1' exists in all three papers

required.point: Encoder networks process the raw (byte-level) input sequence
required.level_why: asks 'What does each stage do?' (encoder)

required.point: The chunking layer (routing module + downsampler) compresses the sequence into fewer vectors using dynamically learned boundaries
required.level_why: each stage (dynamic chunking)
required.level2_parts: the names routing module and downsampler

required.point: The main network processes the compressed sequence and can itself be an H-Net, giving recursive multi-stage hierarchies
required.level_why: each stage (main network)
required.level2_parts: it can itself be an H-Net (recursion)

required.point: The dechunking layer (smoothing module + upsampler) restores the original resolution, combined with a residual Linear(x) from the encoder side
required.level_why: each stage (dechunking)

required.point: Decoder networks process the dechunked sequence back at the original resolution to produce outputs
required.level_why: each stage (decoder)

optional: Inspired by U-Net, but with dynamic rather than fixed-size pooling
Components are stacks of sequence-mixing layers such as Transformers or SSMs

required.point: Routing module: cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs; q_t = W_q x_t, k_t = W_k x_t, p_t = ½(1 − cos(q_t, k_{t−1})), with p_1 = 1
required.level_why: asks 'How does the routing module identify potential chunk boundaries using adjacent representations'
required.level2_parts: the q/k projections and p_t formula; p_1 = 1

required.point: Low similarity at a contextual or semantic shift gives a high boundary probability; boundary indicator b_t = 1 if p_t ≥ 0.5
required.level_why: same: low similarity -> boundary

required.point: Downsampler: keeps the vectors where b_t = 1 and discards those where b_t = 0 (direct selection, chosen over mean/max pooling and cross-attention)
required.level_why: asks 'which vectors does it retain and which does it discard'

required.point: The boundary probabilities are compressed the same way and passed to the dechunking layer
required.level_why: probabilities passed to dechunking is not asked

optional: Smoothing module (EMA) makes boundaries differentiable during training
traps: Do not claim the downsampler has a separate semantic-preservation operation. It directly retains boundary-marked vectors and discards the others; the wider architecture also carries encoder-side residual information through dechunking/decoding.

required.point: Large: Table 2 reports BPE Transformer average accuracy 53.3 and H-Net (2-stage) 55.5; subtracting the displayed values gives a 2.2 percentage-point difference.
required.level_why: asks to compare at 'Large (760M)'

required.point: XL: Table 2 reports BPE Transformer average accuracy 55.5 and H-Net (2-stage) 58.2; subtracting the displayed values gives a 2.7 percentage-point difference.
required.level_why: asks to compare at 'XL (1.3B)'

required.point: The prose in §3.1 states gains of +2.2% at Large and +2.6% at XL. A careful answer identifies that the prose's XL figure differs from the 2.7-point subtraction of the rounded Table 2 averages, and attributes each figure to its source.
required.level_why: asks 'Is there any discrepancy? Attribute each figure to its source.'

optional: H-Net (2-stage) achieves the highest performance across most tasks

The Large H-Net (2-stage) matches the average downstream performance of the XL BPE Transformer (HNET §3.1, Table 2). Moved from required to optional on 2026-11-10 (author): the reworded Q12 no longer asks what the results indicate.
traps: Do not silently present 2.6 and 2.7 as the same figure. The prose says +2.6% at XL; the displayed table averages (58.2 − 55.5) give 2.7 percentage points.
The table labels the baseline 'Transformer (Token)'; §3.1 calls it the BPE Transformer.
'Table 2' exists in all three papers; identify HNET Table 2.

required.point: Positional encoding solves the lack of order information in a model with no recurrence or convolution: fixed sinusoids of position are added to the embeddings
required.level_why: asks 'What problem does each mechanism solve?' (positional encoding)

required.point: Dynamic chunking learns content- and context-dependent segmentation end-to-end, replacing tokenization, and compresses the sequence into chunks
required.level_why: same (dynamic chunking)

required.point: Contrast: positional encoding is fixed (not learned), depends only on position, and leaves sequence length unchanged; dynamic chunking is learned, depends on content (similarity of adjacent representations), and changes sequence length
required.level_why: asks 'How do they differ in terms of injecting sequence structure versus learning content-dependent segmentation?'
required.level2_parts: that only chunking changes sequence length

optional: Learned positional embeddings performed about the same (AIAYN Table 3 (E))
DC allocates compute by compressing low-information regions
traps: Neither paper compares the two mechanisms; every comparative claim must rest on cited facts from each paper

required.point: Causal masking enforces that each output position depends only on earlier positions (positions < i), preserving the auto-regressive property
required.level_why: asks 'What dependency does causal masking enforce'

required.point: Moshi's acoustic delay: a delay of 1 or 2 steps between semantic and acoustic tokens, which gave more stable, higher-quality generation and lets the Temporal Transformer model their inter-dependence
required.level_why: asks 'what purpose do the delay patterns serve' and to distinguish the acoustic delay

required.point: Moshi's text–audio delay decides which modality determines content, giving streaming ASR (audio ahead) or TTS (text ahead)
required.level_why: asks to 'Distinguish ... the text-audio delay used by Inner Monologue'

required.point: Moshi remains autoregressive over time steps: the Temporal Transformer conditions on previous steps
required.level_why: that Moshi stays autoregressive over time steps is not explicitly asked

optional: The delay reduces dependencies between sub-sequences at the same step, so a weaker model can approximate the joint distribution

required.point: Moshi: the Temporal Transformer models the time axis, mapping past steps to a context vector z_s; the smaller Depth Transformer models the K sub-sequences (codebooks/streams) within one step, conditioned on z_s
required.level_why: asks to compare 'Moshi's Temporal Transformer and Depth Transformer'

required.point: Moshi's problem: flattening the codebooks would need about 100 steps per second (30,000 for 5 minutes), which is computationally costly and incompatible with streaming
required.level_why: asks 'what computational or modelling problem is each hierarchy intended to address' (Moshi)

required.point: H-Net: encoder, then chunking that compresses the sequence length with learned boundaries, then the main network on fewer vectors, then dechunking back to the original resolution; stages can nest
required.level_why: asks to compare 'H-Net's encoder, dynamic chunking, main network, dechunking'

required.point: After dechunking, H-Net's decoder network operates on the restored original-resolution sequence and produces the output; decoder layers combine coarse main-network representations with fine-grained encoder residuals.
required.level_why: the question names the decoder; its role on the restored sequence
required.level2_parts: combining coarse output with encoder residuals

required.point: H-Net's problem: replace fixed tokenization with learned end-to-end segmentation and allocate compute by compressing low-information regions
required.level_why: asks 'what computational or modelling problem is each hierarchy intended to address' (author's edit)
required.level1_main: H-Net learns content-dependent segmentation instead of relying on fixed tokenization, which lets computation be allocated adaptively across the sequence.
required.level2_parts: explicitly: low-information regions are compressed while informative regions keep finer granularity

required.point: Contrast: Moshi decomposes the per-step depth (codebook) axis, while H-Net decomposes along sequence length
required.level_why: asks 'What dimensions or structures are being decomposed in each'

optional: Both are cited as RQ-Transformer / hierarchical relatives (Moshi notes a similar approach was suggested for byte-level modeling)

rubric.version: two-level rubric, frozen 2026-11-11 by the author (assistant's draft, approved with two edits)
rubric.level1: Must pass; decides correct or wrong. The answer (a) answers the central question, (b) covers the main idea of every Level 1 point (the explicitly requested components), (c) contains no material factual error, (d) cites passages that actually support its claims, (e) invents nothing absent from the papers.
rubric.level2: Partial credit only, recorded as a diagnostic (point coverage in the trace); it never changes the grade: exact numbers, extra architectural detail, equations and implementation specifics, secondary experimental observations, appendix context. Listed per point as 'level2_parts', or a whole point tagged level 2.
rubric.material_error: A factual error about something the question asks for, or one that changes the meaning.
rubric.no_rescue: Level 2 never rescues an answer with a material factual error: nine right details plus 'tau = 2 means two seconds' is still wrong (author, 2026-11-11). Equally, omitting Level 2 names (e.g. PAD/EPAD) never fails an answer whose core concepts are right.
rubric.unanswerable: Q16-Q20: Level 1 = says the papers do not establish the asked information and gives no value for it; adjacent facts only if cited and framed as not answering.
rubric.rule: The same frozen rubric grades both evaluation runs (eval and eval_v2). It is not modified after seeing the second run's results.
